title: The First Photo From Space
voice_direction: Mark Vale: deep, calm, unhurried American storyteller. Quiet wonder through the climb, a breath before 'it survived', and the last line almost under the breath, no flourish.
narration: The first photograph of Earth from space was taken in nineteen forty-six, by a movie camera mounted inside a captured German missile. After the war, the U.S. Army shipped trainloads of V-2 parts to the New Mexico desert. Scientists swapped the warheads for instruments, and fired the rockets straight up. Until then, the highest photo ever taken came from a balloon, less than fourteen miles up. On the twenty-fourth of October, V-2 number thirteen carried a thirty-five millimeter movie camera. It took one frame every second and a half. The rocket climbed about sixty-five miles, [pause] just past the line we now call the edge of space. Then it fell. It hit the desert so hard the camera was destroyed. But the film was inside a steel cassette. [pause] It survived. One young soldier on the recovery team remembered the scientists jumping up and down like kids. The frames showed the planet, set against the blackness of space. The engineer behind the camera, Clyde Holliday, later wrote that this was how our Earth would look to visitors from another planet. No astronaut. No satellite. Two years earlier, rockets like this one were falling on London. [quietly] The first picture of home from space was taken by a weapon.

instagram_caption:
On 24 October 1946, a V-2 rocket rose straight up from White Sands, New Mexico.

It was a German missile, assembled after the war from captured parts. Where the warhead used to be, engineers had put instruments and a 35 mm movie camera. The camera took one frame every second and a half.

The rocket reached about 65 miles (105 km), just past the 100 km line we now call the edge of space. The highest photo before that came from a balloon, 13.7 miles up.

Then it fell. The camera was smashed in the desert. The film, sealed in a steel cassette, was fine. Fred Rulli, a 19-year-old soldier on the recovery team, remembered the scientists “jumping up and down like kids.”

In 1950, Clyde Holliday, the APL engineer behind the camera, wrote in National Geographic that the pictures showed “how our Earth would look to visitors from another planet coming in on a space ship.”

Less than two years earlier, the same kind of rocket had been falling on London.

What would you send a camera up to photograph? 👇

facts.claim: First photograph of Earth from space: 24 Oct 1946, V-2 no. 13, White Sands, New Mexico
facts.source: Wikipedia 'V-2 No. 13'; Commons file page (US Army/WSMR); Air & Space (Smithsonian), 'The First Photo From Space', Tony Reichhardt, 2006

facts.claim: U.S. V-2s were built from captured German parts; about 300 rail cars of components reached Las Cruces, NM from July 1945; GE reassembled them; first U.S. launch 16 Apr 1946
facts.source: WSMR Museum; Air & Space 'The First Launch of a V-2 Rocket From America'

facts.claim: Instruments and cameras rode in the V-2's warhead / nose section; rockets were fired straight up and fell back minutes later
Before 1946 the highest photos came from the Explorer II balloon, 13.7 miles, 1935
Camera was a 35 mm motion-picture camera (DeVry), developed/adapted by Clyde Holliday of Johns Hopkins APL

facts.source: Commons file description; Holliday (1950) cited in arXiv:1602.02333 as 0.67 Hz
Wikipedia 'V-2 No. 13'; Commons file pages; Air & Space ('65 miles'). Note: Holliday 1950 is cited as ~100 km

facts.claim: Kármán line at 100 km is the FAI convention for the edge of space (a later definition)
Camera smashed on impact; film, protected in a steel cassette, unharmed
Fred Rulli, a 19-year-old enlisted man on the recovery team: 'They were ecstatic, they were jumping up and down like kids.'
facts.source: Air & Space 2006 (wording as repeated by Smithsonian and Ynet; original page not opened)

facts.claim: The V-2 pictures showed the planet set against the blackness of space
Holliday, National Geographic, 1950: the photos showed 'how our Earth would look to visitors from another planet coming in on a space ship'
facts.source: Air & Space 2006; ru.wikipedia (quotes the original English)
